newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heat oil called up on IPE gas oil strength.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heat oil called up on IPE gas oil strength.

text.p: NYMEX heating oil was called higher Tuesday on strength of gas oil futures on London's IPE, while crude was seen drifting lower at the open amid news oil flow stations should reopen in Nigeria Tuesday after being shut due to tribal clashes.

"When oil prices started to go higher last year, gas oil went up first, and it went down first before oil prices came off, so gas oil's action has cast a shadow over the market," said a New York crude trader.
Crude was called steady to five cents a barrel lower. Heat and gasoline were called flat to 0.25 cent a gallon higher.
May gas oil was up $1.50 a tonne at $167.25 on London's IPE after breaking resistance of $167 on fund buying and solid demand from Asia and Latin America, traders said.

A Royal Dutch Shell official said its Nigerian unit is expected to reopen oil flow stations Tuesday after their closures shut in 90,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Forcados crude. Shell was forced to declare force majeure on some cargoes of the blend due for lifting from April 29.
"The Nigeria news should pressure crude a little bit if only because that will mean there is less crude for Shell to force majeure," said Victor Yu, vice president of Refco Inc.
Nigeria accounts for about 10 percent of the seven-to-eight million barrels of crude the U.S. imports daily.
On Monday, June crude ended off eight cents at $19.91 a barrel. May heating oil settled 0.63 cent a gallon higher at 56.53 cents while May gasoline ended 0.16 cent a gallon lower at 62.34 cents.
Dealers will also be anticipating weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) due out after market's close Tuesday. The data reflects the week ended April 25.

Preliminary estimates from traders call for a build in crude stocks of one to three million barrels while a one million barrel decline in distillate stocks is expected. Gasoline stocks are expected to fall one to two million barrels as steady demand was seen offsetting high production.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
